title: The machine was a man in a box.
description:
The machine was a man in a box. Kempelen would open the cabinet, show the clockwork, wind the key. The clockwork was a decoy. A chess master sat behind it on a sliding seat, working the arm with levers.

Built the Turk for the court of Empress Maria Theresa. It beat almost everyone who sat down to play it, and nobody who suspected a hidden operator could prove how it was done.

It beat Franklin. It beat Napoleon. Benjamin Franklin in Paris. Napoleon in Vienna, 1809, who tried illegal moves; the Turk shook its head and put the piece back, then won the game.

It ran for over eighty years. Kempelen died in 1804 and new owners kept it touring. Edgar Allan Poe watched it and wrote that a mind, not a mechanism, was moving the pieces. Fire took it in 1854.

In 2005 Amazon revived the name for humans hidden inside software: "artificial artificial intelligence."

Sources:
- https://www.britannica.com/story/the-mechanical-turk-ai-marvel-or-parlor-trick - Encyclopaedia Britannica, read in full. Established that Wolfgang von Kempelen built the automaton in 1770 for the court of Empress Maria Theresa, the performance format (open the cabinet, show the clockwork, wind the key), that it won most of its games, that Benjamin Franklin played it, that most observers rightly concluded a human operator sat inside working levers, and that Charles Babbage watched it in 1819.
- https://www.history.com/articles/how-a-phony-18th-century-chess-robot-fooled-the-world - History.com (Evan Andrews), read in full. Established that the cabinet's gears were non-functioning decoys hiding a chess master on a sliding seat who followed the game via magnets and worked the arm with levers; that it beat Franklin in Paris and beat Napoleon in Vienna in 1809 (Napoleon tried illegal moves and lost); that Edgar Allan Poe saw it in Richmond and argued a human mind ran it; that Kempelen died in 1804 and Johann Maelzel took it over; and that it burned on 5 July 1854 at Philadelphia's Chinese Museum.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Mechanical_Turk - Via search summary. Established that Amazon launched the Mechanical Turk crowd-work marketplace in 2005, named after the 18th-century chess automaton, and that Jeff Bezos described it as "artificial artificial intelligence" for work done by hidden humans inside software. Corroborated by the paper "The mechanical Turk: a short history of 'artificial artificial intelligence'" (Cultural Studies, 2023).
